# Eval Results

`eval_report.json` in this directory is generated by `python -m eval.run_eval`
and is checked in so the numbers are visible without having to run anything.
Re-run the script and commit the updated file whenever the labeled set or
either scorer changes.

## Lexical baseline (real numbers, generated by actually running the script)
Accuracy: 64.29% Macro-F1: 0.5318
label precision recall f1
grounded 0.50 1.00 0.67
unsupported 0.93 0.93 0.93
contradicted 0.00 0.00 0.00

The one number that matters most here: **0% recall on `contradicted`**. 13 of
14 hand-written contradictions (e.g. claim says "30 days", evidence says "90
days") were scored as `grounded`, because the lexical scorer only measures
token overlap between the claim and the evidence -- a claim that shares most
of its words with the evidence gets a high score whether or not the one
number it changed makes the sentence false. This isn't a tuning problem
(raising the threshold doesn't fix it, it would only trade `unsupported`
errors for different ones) -- it's a structural limitation of the approach:
lexical overlap cannot represent "agrees" vs. "disagrees", only "similar
topic" vs. "different topic". This is the actual, measured justification for
adding the NLI scorer, not just an assumption that a fancier model must be
better.

                    grounded   unsupported  contradicted
grounded                  14             0             0
unsupported                1            13             0
contradicted              13             1             0



```bash
pip install -r requirements-ml.txt
python -m eval.run_eval --scorer nli
# or: python -m eval.run_eval        (runs both side by side)
```

The script runs `_assert_label_order()` first -- three unambiguous
hand-labeled pairs -- and will raise loudly instead of producing numbers if
the model's entailment/contradiction/neutral labels come back in an
unexpected order, so a passing run is itself a basic correctness check, not
just a benchmark.

**Expected direction, not guaranteed numbers:** the NLI scorer should recover
most of the `contradicted` recall the lexical scorer has none of, likely at
some cost to `grounded`/`unsupported` precision on paraphrased or
loosely-worded claims (cross-encoders are more sensitive to phrasing
mismatches that don't affect a bag-of-words score). Report the real numbers
once you've run it -- don't take this paragraph as a substitute for actually
running the script.
